zin: What if you were Joseph Stalin?
You'd start life as the poor son of a shoemaker who beats you.
You'd rob a bank, escape from Siberia, and give yourself a name made of steel.
You'd rule one sixth of the world, and millions would die under your rule.
And when you finally collapse, your own guards would be too afraid to open your door.
So how does a boy from a tiny Georgian town become one of the most feared men in history?
You're born in 1878, in Gori, a small town in Georgia, at the edge of the Russian Empire.
Your name isn't Stalin yet. It's Ioseb Jughashvili, and everybody calls you Soso.
Your father, Beso, is a shoemaker, and he drinks.
When he drinks, he beats you, and he beats your mother.
Your mother, Keke, cleans other people's houses to keep you in school.
At six, you catch smallpox, and it leaves scars on your face for the rest of your life.
At twelve, a horse carriage hits you in the street, and your left arm never fully heals.
But you're clever, you sing in the choir, and you have a fantastic memory.
Your mother has one dream for you: that you become a priest.
In 1894, at fifteen, you go to the seminary in Tiflis, the capital of Georgia.
The rules are strict, and the monks search your room for forbidden books.
You write poems, and some of them are even printed in a Georgian newspaper.
But at night you read what you're not allowed to read: Darwin, Victor Hugo, and Karl Marx.
Marx says the workers will rise up one day, and take everything from the rich.
You like that idea, a lot.
You start skipping prayers and meeting workers in secret.
In 1899, the seminary throws you out.
For a while, you work at the weather station in Tiflis, writing down temperatures every hour.
It's the only normal job you'll ever have.
Then the police raid the weather station, and you go underground.
You give yourself a new name: Koba, after an outlaw hero from a Georgian novel.
You organise strikes, print leaflets, and stir up the oil workers in Baku.
You join the Bolsheviks, the hardest group of revolutionaries, led by Vladimir Lenin.
And the revolution needs money.
In 1907, in the main square of Tiflis, a gang ambushes a coach full of bank money.
Bombs, gunfire, and three hundred and forty-one thousand roubles gone.
Historians still argue how big your role was, but you most likely helped plan it.
The police arrest you again and again.
They send you to Siberia, and you escape.
They send you back, and you escape again.
In 1913, you start signing your articles with a new name: Stalin, the man of steel.
That same year, they send you to the far north of Siberia, almost to the Arctic Ocean.
This time there's no escape, so you spend four years fishing and hunting in the snow.
Then, in 1917, the news reaches your village: the Tsar has fallen.
You take the train back to Petrograd, the capital.
In October, Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power.
Lenin makes you a minister, but the big star is someone else.
Leon Trotsky, a brilliant speaker who builds the Red Army from nothing.
He thinks you're a dull, grey nobody, and he lets everyone know it.
Then civil war breaks out, Reds against Whites, and it lasts for years.
Lenin sends you to Tsaritsyn on the Volga, to get grain to the hungry cities.
You do it with brutal methods, and you never forget who doubted you.
In 1922, you get a job nobody else wants: General Secretary of the party.
It sounds boring, all files and paperwork.
But it means you decide who gets which job, all over the country.
Slowly, everyone owes their career to you.
Then Lenin has a stroke.
From his sickbed, he dictates a secret letter.
Stalin is too rude, he writes, and the comrades should find a way to remove him.
In January 1924, Lenin dies, and the letter is read out to the party leaders.
But nobody acts on it, and you keep your job.
Now you play your rivals against each other, one by one.
First you team up against Trotsky, and push him out of the party.
In 1929, he's thrown out of the country.
Then you turn on the allies who helped you.
By your fiftieth birthday, the whole country is celebrating you.
And you have a plan: to turn a nation of farmers into an industrial giant, in ten years.
New factories, dams and steel cities rise out of empty fields.
But to feed the workers, you need the farmers' grain.
So you take their land, and force them into giant collective farms.
Nearly two million people branded as rich peasants are deported to Siberia and the far north.
Then your men take the grain, even the seed for next year.
In 1932 and 1933, a terrible famine hits Ukraine, Kazakhstan and southern Russia.
Millions of people starve to death, while grain is still being sold abroad.
In November 1932, your wife Nadezhda takes her own life, after a quarrel with you at a dinner.
Officially, she died of appendicitis.
From then on, you trust nobody.
In 1934, Sergei Kirov, a popular party leader, is shot in Leningrad.
You use his murder as a reason to hunt for enemies everywhere.
Old revolutionaries, heroes of 1917, stand in court and confess to crimes they never committed.
Then the secret police get quotas: numbers of enemies to find in every region.
At night, a black car stops outside a building, and someone disappears.
In 1937 and 1938, around seven hundred thousand people are executed.
More than a million others are sent to the Gulag, a chain of labour camps across the country.
Even the army isn't safe: most of its top commanders are shot.
The head of the secret police, Nikolai Yezhov, runs the Terror for you.
Then he's arrested and executed too.
And he quietly disappears from the photos he was in with you.
Trotsky is still alive, in exile in Mexico, writing against you.
In 1940, one of your agents finally reaches him, and kills him.
In 1939, you shock the world: you sign a pact with Adolf Hitler.
In secret, you agree to split Eastern Europe between you.
Your spies warn you that Hitler is going to attack.
You refuse to believe them.
On the twenty-second of June, 1941, three million German soldiers cross the border.
Your army collapses, and the Germans race toward Moscow.
But you stay in the city, and in November, you hold the parade on Red Square anyway.
The soldiers march straight from the square to the front.
Your oldest son, Yakov, is captured by the Germans.
Later, they offer to trade him for a German field marshal.
According to the story, you answer: I don't trade a soldier for a field marshal.
Yakov dies in a German camp, in 1943.
At Stalingrad, the city named after you, a whole German army is surrounded and destroyed.
In 1945, Soviet soldiers raise the red flag over Berlin.
You've won, but around twenty-seven million Soviet people are dead.
Now you rule half of Europe, and soon you have the atomic bomb.
Your face is on posters, in schools, and on statues in every town.
But at home, you get more and more paranoid.
In 1953, you accuse your own doctors of a plot to poison the leaders.
On the first of March, at your country house near Moscow, you collapse.
Your guards have strict orders: nobody disturbs you.
So they wait, all day, too afraid to open the door.
When they finally go in, late that evening, you're lying on the floor.
Four days later, on the fifth of March 1953, you die, at seventy-four.
Millions cry in the streets, and at your funeral, people are crushed to death in the crowds.
Three years later, your successor, Nikita Khrushchev, gives a secret speech.
He tells the party what you really did.
Your statues come down, and your body is removed from Lenin's tomb.
Even Stalingrad gets a new name: Volgograd.
You took a poor farming country, and turned it into a superpower with the bomb.
But millions paid for it with their lives.
And to this day, people still argue whether you were a hero or a monster.
